blocks.text: “Hi hi!” said the old man coming to the door. “Have you anything to sell?”

Naturally, we stepped back and looked at the woman who had brought us there. She had been trying to open the house door with a key from her pocket. Richard now told her that we had enjoyed seeing where she lived. But we had little time, so we would leave her now. She would not let us leave so easily. She begged us to come upstairs and see her rooms for just a moment. Her manner was strangely eager, and she kept pressing us. In her harmless way, she was determined to lead me inside. This was part of the sign of good luck she wanted. Whatever the others might do, I felt I had no choice but to agree. I suppose we were all curious to some degree. At any rate, the old man joined her in trying to persuade us. “Yes, yes! Please her! It won't take a minute! Come in, come in! Come in through the shop, if the other door won't work!” So we all went in. Richard laughed and encouraged us, and we trusted him to protect us.

“My landlord, Krook,” said the little old lady as she introduced him to us. She spoke as if she were far above him in importance. “The neighbours call him the Lord Chancellor. His shop is called the Court of Chancery. He behaves in very unusual ways. He is very strange. Oh, I promise you, he is very strange!”

She shook her head many times and tapped her forehead with her finger. She meant that we must be kind enough to excuse him. “For he is a little—you know!—M—!” said the old lady, with a very grand manner. The old man heard her and laughed.

“It's true enough,” he said, going before us with the lantern, “that they call me the Lord Chancellor, and call my shop Chancery. And why do you think they call me the Lord Chancellor, and my shop Chancery?”
“I don't know, I am sure!” said Richard, rather carelessly.

“You see,” said the old man, stopping and turning round, “they—Hi! Here's lovely hair! I have three sacks of ladies' hair down below. But none of it is as beautiful and fine as this. What a color! And how it feels!”

“That's enough, my good friend!” said Richard. The old man had pulled a lock of Ada's hair through his yellow hand. Richard strongly disapproved of this. “You can admire it as the rest of us do, without touching it like that.”

The old man suddenly shot a look at Richard. It even drew my attention away from Ada. She was surprised and blushing, and so very beautiful that even the little old lady seemed unable to look away. Usually, the lady's attention wandered from one thing to another. But Ada spoke up with a laugh. She said she could only feel proud that someone admired her so sincerely. Mr. Krook then seemed to shrink back into his usual self, as suddenly as he had jumped out of it.

“You see, I have so many things here,” he went on, holding up the lantern. “There are so many different kinds. The neighbours think they are all slowly falling apart and being ruined. But they know nothing. That's why they've given these names to me and my place. And I have so many old documents written on animal skin, and so many papers in my stock. And I like rust and the smell of damp old things and cobwebs. And any fish that comes into my net is welcome. And once I get hold of anything, I can't bear to let it go. Or so my neighbours think, but what do they know? And I can't bear to change anything. I can't bear any sweeping, scrubbing, cleaning or repairs going on around me. That's how I got the bad name of Chancery. I don't mind. I go to see my brother, that great and learned man, almost every day when he holds court in the Inn. He doesn't notice me, but I notice him. There's no great difference between us. We both keep digging away in a mess. Hi, Lady Jane!”
